newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: YEAREND-Private banks eye riches in emerging world.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Private banks eye riches in emerging world.

text.p: Switzerland's private bankers, their cozy world disrupted by the arrival of new kids on the block, expect tough competition in 1997 but are confident that business will grow on new wealth created in the emerging world.

Swiss private bankers, who share the market with such Wall Street powerhouses as Merrill Lynch and JP Morgan, forecast assets under management to grow by at least 15 percent in 1997, helped by a growing wealth base in the Far East and East Europe.
Professionalism and performance will be the name of the game in 1997 as competition increases and clients get fussier, a trend likely to bring mergers and new alliances, bankers said.

Pierre Darier, managing partner at Darier Hentsch & Cie, said old private banks had expertise and a kudos that bigger banks lacked in Switzerland, where he put the rise in liquid private wealth under management at 20 percent in 1996.
"There's competition, but we're used to it. Everyone's trying to do what we've done for 200 years," he said. "Bigger banks offer quality service, but we bring humanity to banking."
Pierre Poncet, managing partner at Bordier & Cie, added: "We're optimistic about 1997. We are in a growing business segment and Switzerland is attracting more clients."

With multi-lingual services, shopping centres, summer and winter holiday resorts close by, and a good airport, Geneva is a world centre for private banking, a strong growth area for domestic and international banks.

There are no officially published figures, but informal estimates put the total amount of private capital stored by foreign residents in Switzerland at more than $2 trillion -- or nearly half of the international offshore wealth.
INVESTMENT PROFILE IS CHANGING, COMPETITION IS RISING
But it's a far different world from the days when a neutral status, political stability and low taxes ensured Switzerland's status at the top of the world's private banking league.
"You can't talk about the weather and offer a cup of coffee to the client any more," said Serge Robin, a member of senior management and head of research at Lombard Odier & Cie.
"Clients are becoming more professional. They ask about global returns, how to control risk and get highest yields."

Investors demand more and a swarm of newcomers are jostling for a smaller, more risk-averse pool of capital as the profile of new clients changes drastically. Some banks no longer ask for a minimum $1 million investment. Some demand just $100,000.
PROSPECTS GOOD IN ASIA, WEALTH GROWTH SLOWING IN EUROPE
Bankers said Geneva was a magnet in 1996 for capital flying out of Hong Kong ahead of the colony's reintegration with China next year.
"We had a good flow of money from Hong Kong this year," said Pictet & Cie's Beguelin.

Robin at Lombard Odier said growth in the European client base, mainly created through inheritance of fortunes by middle-aged professionals as parents die, would slow down in 1997 while the private wealth base in the Far East would expand.
Bordier & Cie's Poncet said the Far East and eastern Europe would be growth areas for private banks in 1997.
"China is the next growth market. There is a lot of money in Hong Kong," he said. "We're also starting to have clients from eastern European countries. It's a new area of growth."
"Wealth profiles are changing. The clientele is getting older in continental Europe. In eastern Europe, the clients are younger -- entrepreneurs and new rich families."
Poncet said his bank was responding to changing wealth profiles by being more aggressive and performance-oriented.

Darier said Darier Hentsch & Cie was attacking new markets both abroad and at home, where it opened a new office in Lugano in Italian-speaking south-east Switzerland to handle the lucrative private wealth coming across the border from Italy.
BANKS EXPANDING PORTFOLIO MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS
To become competitive, banks are trying to do more business overseas where they need an international culture of deal-making and move away from the traditional conservative Swiss approach.
This year, Switzerland's leading private bank Pictet & Cie launched a new Polish investment fund worth up to $50 million jointly with Poland's Bank Rozowoju Eksportu SA.
Swissca, the investment joint venture of Swiss cantonal banks, signed a deal with the Commercial Bank of Greece to market its mutual funds in Greece and Cyprus.
And Bank Julis Baer opened a new office in Vienna.
"In the past, clients just came. Now, we have to go out and look for them," said Jean-Pierre Beguelin, member of senior management and chief economist at Pictet & Cie.
